titleStmt.title: Food waste within food supply chains: quantification and potential for change to 2050
titleStmt.author: Julian Parfitt
Mark Barthel
Sarah J. Macnaughton

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Food waste within food supply chains: quantification and potential for change to 2050
bibl.publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: food waste and post-harvest loss across the global food supply chain, from harvest to the household bin, and what is actually known about how much there is
span.quote: Food waste in the global food supply chain is reviewed in relation to the prospects for feeding a population of nine billion by 2050.

span.label: how much food is lost or wasted globally, at which stages, and whether the existing evidence can support any answer
span.quote: An international literature review found a dearth of data on food waste and estimates varied widely; those for post-harvest losses of grain in developing countries might be overestimated.

span.label: a review finding that no firm global evidence base exists - the quoted ranges all trace back to the same 1970s-80s datasets - together with a three-way definitional clarification and expert-interview evidence
span.quote: Ranges between 10 and 40 percent of total global food production and as high as 50 per cent are quoted, but on closer examination, these estimates all link back to the same limited primary datasets, where much of the published data relates to fieldwork undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s.

span.label: critique
span.quote: As a consequence of the information gaps and uncertainties, there is no consensus on the proportion of global food production that is currently lost.

span.label: food lost or discarded between harvest and consumption, at a scale nobody can presently quantify
span.quote: As much of the post-harvest loss data for developing countries was collected over 30 years ago, current global losses cannot be quantified.

span.label: a driver review combining the international literature on food waste with interviews of international food-supply-chain experts
span.term: a driver review combining the international literature on food waste with interviews of international food-supply-chain experts
span.quote: This paper presents results from a driver review of food waste issues, combining information on food waste from the international literature and interviews with supply chain experts.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WHICH WORD A STUDY USES COMMITS IT TO A REMEDY: `loss` is post-harvest and points at infrastructure investment; `waste` is post-consumer and points at behavioural change. The definitional choice is therefore also a policy choice, made before any measurement
span.quote: Within the literature, food waste post-harvest is likely to be referred to as ‘food losses’ and ‘spoilage’. Food loss refers to the decrease in food quantity or quality, which makes it unfit for human consumption (Grolleaud 2002). At later stages of the FSC, the term food waste is applied and generally relates to behavioural issues. Food losses/spoilage, conversely, relate to systems that require investment in infrastructure.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: COSMETIC STANDARDS MANUFACTURE LOSS IN RICH COUNTRIES: grain losses were engineered out by technological investment, while retailer and consumer demand for cosmetically perfect fruit and vegetables creates out-grades - so industrialised post-harvest loss moved rather than fell
span.quote: In the industrialized world meanwhile, post-harvest losses have been squeezed out of grain supply through heavy technological investments, while for FFVs, retailers' and consumers' demand for ‘cosmetically perfect’ produce has created significant post-harvest losses through ‘out-grades’.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE RESEARCH FUNDING IS WHERE THE LOSSES ARE NOT: under 5% of agricultural research funding goes to post-harvest systems, which is where developing-country losses are concentrated and where loss reduction is agreed to matter for food security
span.quote: Less than 5 per cent of the funding for agricultural research is allocated to post-harvest systems (Kader 2003), and yet reduction of these losses is recognized as an important component of improved food security

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SUPPLY CHANGE OUTRUNS INFRASTRUCTURE: fresh fruit and vegetables expanded rapidly in transitional countries without the cold chain to carry them, so the post-harvest loss follows the market rather than the technology
span.note: status: is highly likely to have resulted in
span.quote: The rapid expansion of FFVs supplied to consumers in transitional countries is highly likely to have resulted in significant post-harvest losses, owing to inadequate infrastructure.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A COHORT EFFECT MISREAD AS AN AGE EFFECT: today's lowest wasters are the immediate post-war generation, and the paper warns that tomorrow's elderly will carry today's attitudes forward - so the demographic gradient does not project
span.quote: However, it would be a mistake to assume that the demographic distribution will remain the same in the future, as today's elderly generally exhibit a ‘waste not want not’ mentality, while the elderly of the future are likely to continue to retain the same attitudes and behaviours to food that they have today.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: EVERY GLOBAL FIGURE SHARES ITS SOURCES: the 10-50% range comes from estimates that all link back to the same limited primary datasets from 1970s and 1980s fieldwork, so the spread between published figures measures re-extrapolation rather than disagreement between independent measurements
span.quote: Ranges between 10 and 40 percent of total global food production and as high as 50 per cent are quoted, but on closer examination, these estimates all link back to the same limited primary datasets, where much of the published data relates to fieldwork undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s.

span.label: a firm global evidence base does not exist; much of the developing-country loss data was collected over 30 years ago
span.quote: A firm evidence base from which to assess food waste globally is lacking, with no specific information on the impact of food waste in BRIC countries a major concern, and with much of the loss estimates from developing countries collected over 30 years ago.

span.label: current global losses cannot be quantified at all on the available data
span.quote: As much of the post-harvest loss data for developing countries was collected over 30 years ago, current global losses cannot be quantified.

span.label: there is no consensus on what proportion of global food production is lost
span.quote: As a consequence of the information gaps and uncertainties, there is no consensus on the proportion of global food production that is currently lost.

span.label: the quoted range of 10-40% and up to 50% traces back to the same limited primary datasets from 1970s and 1980s fieldwork
span.quote: Ranges between 10 and 40 percent of total global food production and as high as 50 per cent are quoted, but on closer examination, these estimates all link back to the same limited primary datasets, where much of the published data relates to fieldwork undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s.

span.label: a significant gap exists for the rapidly developing BRIC economies, which no dataset covers
span.quote: A significant gap exists in the understanding of the food waste implications of the rapid development of ‘BRIC’ economies.

span.label: post-harvest grain losses in developing countries are likely to be over-stated in the existing literature
span.quote: Recent reviewers of these data claim there is a tendency to over-state losses in relation to traditional agricultural systems in developing countries, a point reiterated in this review.

span.label: without systematic evidence the debate remains rhetorical and progress against any reduction target cannot be measured - the paper says its own field cannot currently check itself
span.quote: Without systematic evidence, the arguments over the potential for reducing global food waste as a contribution to feeding nine billion people by 2050 will remain largely rhetorical, and measuring progress against any global reduction target impossible.

span.label: existing assessments rest on limited datasets gathered at different times and extrapolated upward to a global picture
span.quote: Such assessments are reliant on limited datasets collected across the food supply chain (FSC) at different times and extrapolated to the larger picture.

span.label: food waste is most readily defined only at the retail and consumer stages, where the material is self-evidently food - which is why upstream definitions vary
span.quote: Food waste occurs at different points in the FSC, although it is most readily defined at the retail and consumer stages, where outputs of the agricultural system are self-evidently ‘food’ for human consumption.

span.label: definitions are set by legal jurisdiction and framed around specific environmental controls, so they are not comparable across countries
span.quote: Although waste is formally defined in different legal jurisdictions, definitions relate to particular points of arising and are often framed in relation to specific environmental controls.

span.label: the paper states which of the three definitions it uses and on what condition - the second only where nutritional assessment of animal feed and processing by-products is available - so its own numbers are scoped before they are given
span.note: eliminates: the ambiguity of `food waste` as a source of the review's own numbers - the paper states which of three definitions it uses and on what condition · outcome: held
span.quote: The first two definitions are considered to be most relevant, although the second can only be supported if data are available that include nutritional assessment of animal feed and food processing by-products.

span.label: expert interviews were used to supplement the literature precisely because the documentary picture is fragmentary, rather than as a primary source
span.note: eliminates: the fragmentary documentary record being taken as the whole picture - expert interviews were added precisely because it is fragmentary, though they are a supplement and not a measurement · outcome: partial
span.quote: To supplement the fragmentary picture and to gain a forward view, interviews were conducted with international FSC experts.

span.label: the household figures are bounded to household disposal routes, explicitly excluding food eaten on-the-go, at work or in catering
span.note: eliminates: food eaten on-the-go, at work or in catering being silently counted in a household figure - the scope is bounded to household disposal routes · outcome: held
span.quote: Sources of food and drinks that are consumed within the home include retail and contributions from home-grown food and takeaways. Figure 3 indicates which disposal routes are classified as household waste streams. In effect, this excludes significant quantities of food and drink eaten ‘on-the-go’, in the workplace or in catering establishments.

span.label: food waste
span.quote: An international literature review found a dearth of data on food waste and estimates varied widely; those for post-harvest losses of grain in developing countries might be overestimated.

span.label: food losses
span.quote: Within the literature, food waste post-harvest is likely to be referred to as ‘food losses’ and ‘spoilage’. Food loss refers to the decrease in food quantity or quality, which makes it unfit for human consumption (Grolleaud 2002). At later stages of the FSC, the term food waste is applied and generally relates to behavioural issues. Food losses/spoilage, conversely, relate to systems that require investment in infrastructure.

span.label: post-harvest
span.quote: The limited data suggest that losses are much higher at the immediate post-harvest stages in developing countries and higher for perishable foods across industrialized and developing economies alike.

span.label: post-consumer food waste
span.quote: For affluent economies, post-consumer food waste accounts for the greatest overall losses.

span.label: over-nutrition
span.quote: As definitions (1) and (2) but including over-nutrition—the gap between the energy value of _consumed_ food _per capita_ and the energy value of food _needed per capita_ (Smil 2004 _a_).

span.label: out-grades
span.quote: In the industrialized world meanwhile, post-harvest losses have been squeezed out of grain supply through heavy technological investments, while for FFVs, retailers' and consumers' demand for ‘cosmetically perfect’ produce has created significant post-harvest losses through ‘out-grades’.

span.label: market transformation
span.quote: Linked to the above, market transformation has enormous potential to develop FSC infrastructure and reduce waste in developing and BRIC countries.

span.label: driver review
span.quote: This paper presents results from a driver review of food waste issues, combining information on food waste from the international literature and interviews with supply chain experts.

span.label: food security
span.quote: Less than 5 per cent of the funding for agricultural research is allocated to post-harvest systems (Kader 2003), and yet reduction of these losses is recognized as an important component of improved food security

span.label: infrastructure
span.quote: The lack of infrastructure in many developing countries and poor harvesting/growing techniques are likely to remain major elements in the generation of food waste.

span.label: the proportion of household income spent on food → the amount of food wasted
span.note: AN INVERSE ASSOCIATION REPORTED ACROSS A LITERATURE, not a measured effect of this study: `as the proportion of income spent on food declines, food waste increases`. It is the majority finding of many studies rather than one design, and the vocabulary has no `associated-with` - see Q-879. `causes` would assert a mechanism this review does not test.
span.quote: The majority of studies show that as the proportion of income spent on food declines, food waste increases.

span.label: food waste - THE PAPER ENUMERATES THREE COMPETING DEFINITIONS AND SAYS WHICH IT USES, which is rare enough to be the reason this record is worth holding. (1) FAO 1981: wholesome edible material intended for human consumption, discarded, lost, degraded or eaten by pests anywhere in the chain. (2) Stuart 2009: as (1) PLUS edible material fed to animals or diverted as a processing by-product. (3) Smil 2004: as (1) and (2) PLUS OVER-NUTRITION - the gap between energy consumed and energy needed. The paper adopts the first two and states that the second is only usable where nutritional data on animal feed exist
span.quote: As definitions (1) and (2) but including over-nutrition—the gap between the energy value of _consumed_ food _per capita_ and the energy value of food _needed per capita_ (Smil 2004 _a_).

span.label: food waste vs food LOSS - NOT SYNONYMS AND THE DIFFERENCE IS WHERE THE REMEDY GOES. `Food loss` is used post-harvest and names a decrease in quantity or quality; `food waste` is used at the consumer end and relates to behaviour. Losses want investment in infrastructure, waste wants behavioural change - so which word a study uses commits it to a class of intervention
span.quote: Within the literature, food waste post-harvest is likely to be referred to as ‘food losses’ and ‘spoilage’. Food loss refers to the decrease in food quantity or quality, which makes it unfit for human consumption (Grolleaud 2002). At later stages of the FSC, the term food waste is applied and generally relates to behavioural issues. Food losses/spoilage, conversely, relate to systems that require investment in infrastructure.

span.label: household food waste - A THREE-WAY CLASSIFICATION, `avoidable`, `possibly avoidable` and `unavoidable`, and a bounded scope: it counts only what is disposed of through household streams, which EXCLUDES food eaten on-the-go, at work or in catering. A household figure is therefore not a per-person figure
span.quote: Wherever possible, the distinction is made between three classifications of household food waste (figure 4): ‘avoidable’, ‘possibly avoidable’ and ‘unavoidable’.

span.label: the `half of all food is wasted` figure - THE MOST QUOTED ESTIMATE IN THE FIELD AND THE PAPER TREATS IT AS UNSCRUTINISABLE. It is cited here as the received claim being examined, not as a finding of this review, and the review's own conclusion is that the range 10-50% traces back to one limited set of 1970s-80s fieldwork
span.quote: The most often quoted estimate is that ‘as much as half of all food grown is lost or wasted before and after it reaches the consumer’ (Lundqvist _et al_. 2008).

span.label: critiques → the most-quoted estimate that as much as half of all food grown is lost or wasted (Lundqvist et al. 2008), which the paper says is difficult to scrutinise
span.quote: The most often quoted estimate is that ‘as much as half of all food grown is lost or wasted before and after it reaches the consumer’ (Lundqvist _et al_. 2008).

span.label: critiques → post-harvest loss estimates for grain in developing countries, which recent reviewers say are over-stated and which this review says so again
span.note: differs in: the paper does not produce a corrected figure - it argues the existing ones cannot be scrutinised, which is a weaker and more careful position than a replacement estimate
span.quote: Recent reviewers of these data claim there is a tendency to over-state losses in relation to traditional agricultural systems in developing countries, a point reiterated in this review.

span.label: distinguishes-from → Smil's definition of food waste, which includes over-nutrition; the paper reports it and adopts the two narrower definitions instead
span.quote: The first two definitions are considered to be most relevant, although the second can only be supported if data are available that include nutritional assessment of animal feed and food processing by-products.

span.label: food losses —distinct-from→ food waste
span.quote: Within the literature, food waste post-harvest is likely to be referred to as ‘food losses’ and ‘spoilage’. Food loss refers to the decrease in food quantity or quality, which makes it unfit for human consumption (Grolleaud 2002). At later stages of the FSC, the term food waste is applied and generally relates to behavioural issues. Food losses/spoilage, conversely, relate to systems that require investment in infrastructure.

span.label: out-grades —causes→ post-harvest
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: In the industrialized world meanwhile, post-harvest losses have been squeezed out of grain supply through heavy technological investments, while for FFVs, retailers' and consumers' demand for ‘cosmetically perfect’ produce has created significant post-harvest losses through ‘out-grades’.

span.label: infrastructure —causes→ food waste
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The lack of infrastructure in many developing countries and poor harvesting/growing techniques are likely to remain major elements in the generation of food waste.

span.label: market transformation —causes→ food waste
span.note: status: has enormous potential to · direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: Linked to the above, market transformation has enormous potential to develop FSC infrastructure and reduce waste in developing and BRIC countries.

span.label: no consensus exists on the proportion of global food production lost, and the 10-50% range quoted all traces to the same 1970s-80s primary data
span.quote: Ranges between 10 and 40 percent of total global food production and as high as 50 per cent are quoted, but on closer examination, these estimates all link back to the same limited primary datasets, where much of the published data relates to fieldwork undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s.

span.label: losses are highest immediately post-harvest in developing countries and highest for perishables everywhere; in affluent economies post-consumer waste dominates
span.quote: The limited data suggest that losses are much higher at the immediate post-harvest stages in developing countries and higher for perishable foods across industrialized and developing economies alike.

span.label: as the share of income spent on food falls, food waste rises
span.quote: The majority of studies show that as the proportion of income spent on food declines, food waste increases.

span.label: waste is distributed across demographic groups with the lowest rates in the immediate post-war generation - which the authors warn is a cohort effect and will not project forward
span.quote: However, it would be a mistake to assume that the demographic distribution will remain the same in the future, as today's elderly generally exhibit a ‘waste not want not’ mentality, while the elderly of the future are likely to continue to retain the same attitudes and behaviours to food that they have today.

span.label: food waste (FAO 1981)
span.quote: Wholesome edible material intended for human consumption, arising at any point in the FSC that is instead discarded, lost, degraded or consumed by pests (FAO 1981).

span.label: food waste (Stuart 2009)
span.quote: As (1), but including edible material that is intentionally fed to animals or is a by-product of food processing diverted away from the human food (Stuart 2009).

span.label: food waste (Smil 2004)
span.quote: As definitions (1) and (2) but including over-nutrition—the gap between the energy value of _consumed_ food _per capita_ and the energy value of food _needed per capita_ (Smil 2004 _a_).

span.label: food losses
span.quote: Within the literature, food waste post-harvest is likely to be referred to as ‘food losses’ and ‘spoilage’. Food loss refers to the decrease in food quantity or quality, which makes it unfit for human consumption (Grolleaud 2002). At later stages of the FSC, the term food waste is applied and generally relates to behavioural issues. Food losses/spoilage, conversely, relate to systems that require investment in infrastructure.

span.label: household food waste
span.quote: Wherever possible, the distinction is made between three classifications of household food waste (figure 4): ‘avoidable’, ‘possibly avoidable’ and ‘unavoidable’.

span.label: quoted global loss ranges of 10-40% of food production, and as high as 50% — None
span.quote: Ranges between 10 and 40 percent of total global food production and as high as 50 per cent are quoted, but on closer examination, these estimates all link back to the same limited primary datasets, where much of the published data relates to fieldwork undertaken in the 1970s and 1980s.

span.quote: Less than 5 per cent of the funding for agricultural research is allocated to post-harvest systems (Kader 2003), and yet reduction of these losses is recognized as an important component of improved food security

span.label: developing-country post-harvest loss data collected over 30 years ago — None
span.quote: As much of the post-harvest loss data for developing countries was collected over 30 years ago, current global losses cannot be quantified.

span.quote: Food waste in the global food supply chain is reviewed in relation to the prospects for feeding a population of nine billion by 2050.

span.term: stage of the food supply chain at which loss arises, harvest through post-consumer
span.quote: The limited data suggest that losses are much higher at the immediate post-harvest stages in developing countries and higher for perishable foods across industrialized and developing economies alike.

span.quote: The majority of studies show that as the proportion of income spent on food declines, food waste increases.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2010.0126.
